book.title: How to Live on Twenty-Four Hours a Day (English)
book.author: Arnold Bennett

overview.summary: The book argues that everyone receives exactly twenty-four hours each day, yet most people never budget this income even though it cannot be earned back. It begins by showing that time, unlike money, is distributed equally and cannot be repaired by borrowing or earning, so daily expenditure must be examined minute by minute. The unease many feel comes from wanting to do something beyond obligatory duties but never beginning; before starting, one must accept difficulty, begin at once, and start small. The central mistake is treating the paid job as the whole day and letting the sixteen hours outside it drain away; the remedy is to protect the morning train and ninety minutes every other evening for consecutive mental cultivation. The book then trains concentration and the reflective mood, extends cultivation to the arts and to perceiving cause and effect, and defines serious reading by the strain it imposes. It closes by warning against self-importance, rigidity, and rush, recommending a modest programme held lightly.
keyIdeas: Everyone gets the same twenty-four hours daily; time is the one income that cannot be increased or repaid.
The trouble is not too few hours but an unstarted wish to do something beyond obligatory duties.
Treat the sixteen hours outside the job as a day within a day and protect a small, regular programme of mental cultivation.
The mind can be trained by concentration and then applied to daily self-examination.
Art, cause-and-effect, and serious reading supply material for cultivation, but only strain and reflection make it count.
Attempt less, start slowly, and hold the programme lightly to avoid priggishness, rigidity, and rush.
overview.mindmap:
# How to Live on Twenty-Four Hours a Day (English)
## The Daily Miracle
- Twenty-four hours are issued equally each morning.
- Time cannot be earned back or borrowed.
- Daily expenditure must be examined minute by minute.
## The Desire To Exceed One's Programme
- Unease comes from an unstarted wish beyond duties.
- Attempt matters more than success.
- The outside wish is often the desire for knowledge.
## Precautions Before Beginning
- Accept that the task is hard.
- Begin at once; every hour arrives fresh.
- Start small to avoid burnt-out ardour.
## The Cause Of The Troubles
- Do not treat the ten-to-six job as the whole day.
- The sixteen hours outside work belong to body, soul, and others.
- Small intervals drain away unseen.
## Tennis And The Immortal Soul
- Reclaim the morning train from newspapers.
- Fatigue is a habit; shape the evening and it disappears.
- Guard ninety minutes every other evening for mental cultivation.
## Remember Human Nature
- Aim at seven and a half hours a week over six days.
- Treat extra time as a windfall.
- Begin humbly and judge after three months.
## Controlling The Mind
- The mind can be trained like a muscle.
- Choose a subject when leaving the house and haul attention back.
- Concentrate on something worth thinking about.
## The Reflective Mood
- Concentration is only preliminary.
- Examine your happiness, direction, principles, and conduct.
- Books can shape principles but cannot replace daily self-examination.
## Interest In The Arts
- Reject the false choice of literature or nothing.
- Learn the art you already enjoy with a primer.
- Select concerts and specialise after hunting for detail.
## Nothing In Life Is Humdrum
- Perceive that nothing happens without a cause.
- Causation makes human behaviour and the world less monotonous.
- Study your own trade's causes for zest.
## Serious Reading
- Mental cultivation depends on strain.
- Poetry comes first; history or philosophy if poetry repels.
- Confine the subject and give at least forty-five minutes of reflection.
## Dangers To Avoid
- Do not become a prig about your system.
- Do not worship or neglect the programme.
- Attempt less rather than rush.

chapters.title: The Daily Miracle
chapters.tldr: Everyone is issued exactly twenty-four hours each morning, equally and without fail, yet nobody budgets them — and unlike money, a shortfall of time can never be made up.
chapters.summary:
Newspapers print endless advice on living on a given income of money, but never on living on a given income of time — even though time is worth more, since money can be earned with time while no wealth buys back a single minute. Time is the raw material of everything: with it all is possible, without it nothing.

Every morning the purse is refilled with twenty-four hours, distributed with perfect equality: genius gets no extra hour and waste is never cut off at the meter, nor can you borrow against tomorrow. That is the daily miracle. And because a shortfall of time, unlike a shortfall of money, cannot be repaired by earning, borrowing or asking, most people merely muddle through, their great spending departments unmanaged. Since we shall never have more time than we have now, daily expenditure of time must be examined minute by minute.

cards.title: Nobody writes about living on time
cards.body: Newspapers endlessly print advice on living on a given income of money, but never on living on a given income of time — even though time is worth far more than money, since money can be earned with time but never buys back a minute.
cards.details: The proverb "time is money" understates the case: if you have time you can usually obtain money, but with all the wealth in the world you cannot buy yourself one minute more than anyone else has, or than the cat by the fire has. Philosophers have explained space, not time; it is the inexplicable raw material of everything — with it all is possible, without it nothing. Yet the enterprising newspapers, full of "How to live on such-and-such a sum," print no essay on how to live on twenty-four hours a day.

cards.title: The daily miracle of twenty-four hours
cards.body: Every morning your purse is magically refilled with twenty-four hours of the raw material of your life. The commodity is unstealable, perfectly equally distributed, and never withheld however badly you waste it.
cards.details: In the realm of time there is no aristocracy of wealth or of intellect: genius is never rewarded with an extra hour, and there is no punishment either — waste as much as you like and no power cuts you off at the meter. Payment is more certain than consols and is not affected by Sundays. Nor can you draw on the future or get into debt: you can only waste the passing moment; tomorrow and the next hour are kept for you. That is what makes the arrangement a miracle.

cards.title: A time deficit cannot be earned back
cards.body: A money shortfall can be fixed by earning more, stealing, or advertising for it; a time shortfall cannot be fixed at all, so failing to make twenty-four hours cover your proper expenditure muddles your life definitely.
cards.details: Run short of a thousand pounds a year and you brace your muscles, make it guineas, and balance the budget. Run short of time and there is no equivalent move: the supply is gloriously regular but cruelly restricted, and no one lives on twenty-four hours a day — most merely exist or muddle through, with the "great spending departments" of their life unmanaged, a fine suit crowned by a shameful hat. The remedy begins with the neglected truth that we never shall have any more time than we have now, which is why the writer turns to a minute practical examination of daily time-expenditure.

cards.body: Why can a badly managed budget of money be repaired while a badly managed budget of twenty-four hours cannot?
cards.answer: Because money is far commoner than time: if your income won't cover your needs you can earn a little more, steal it, or advertise for it, and balance the budget. Time admits no such move — the supply is fixed, unstealable and cannot be drawn on in advance, so a shortfall in time leaves life permanently muddled.

cards.body: You get twenty-four hours every morning, equally, unfailingly, and with no debt allowed against tomorrow. Unlike money, a shortfall of time can never be made up — so the only remedy is to stop muddling through and examine, minute by minute, where your daily expenditure of time actually goes.

flashcards.q: Why is the proverb "time is money" an understatement rather than a fair description?
flashcards.a: Because if you have time you can usually obtain money, but all the wealth in the world cannot buy you one extra minute beyond what everyone else has.

flashcards.q: What makes the daily issue of twenty-four hours a "miracle"?
flashcards.a: It arrives fresh every morning, is distributed with perfect equality regardless of wealth or genius, is never withheld however badly it is wasted, and cannot be overdrawn against tomorrow.

flashcards.q: Why is falling short of time more serious than falling short of money?
flashcards.a: A money shortfall can be met by earning more, stealing or advertising for it; a time shortfall admits no equivalent move, so the life stays permanently muddled.

flashcards.q: If your days feel too short for everything you ought to do, what first step does the chapter point to?
flashcards.a: Accept that you will never have any more time than the twenty-four hours you have now, and begin a minute practical examination of how you actually spend them.

chapters.title: The Desire To Exceed One's Programme
chapters.tldr: The chapter's restlessness comes not from too few hours but from an unmet wish to do something beyond one's obligatory programme — and from never having even begun.
chapters.summary:
The chapter's complaint is not too few hours but a persistent unease that years slip by while life stays out of order — an aspiration that interrupts theatre laughter and the last-train wait with the question of what you have done with your youth.

The torment belongs to the man who desires Mecca and never leaves Brixton, not to one who sets out and may drown: attempt matters, not success. Most never ask the price of the tour, hiding behind twenty-four hours. Behind the unease is a fixed idea that something be done beyond obligatory duties; until effort is made, one waits for something unstarted, and duties met — health, debts, savings — leave the skeleton present. That outside wish, often literary, is the desire for knowledge.

cards.title: Uneasy Aspiration, Not Time Scarcity
cards.body: The chapter's complaint is not that twenty-four hours are too few for duties and pleasures. It is a constant uneasiness that the years are slipping by while life remains out of working order.
cards.details: This feeling is expectation and aspiration, and it behaves like a skeleton at the feast: it interrupts theatre laughter between acts and, while you wait for the last train, asks what you have done with your youth and age. The narrator grants that looking forward is part of life, but insists there are degrees of torment.

cards.title: Leaving Brixton Versus Reaching Mecca
cards.body: A man who sets out for Mecca may drown or never arrive, but he is not as tormented as the man who desires Mecca and never leaves Brixton.
cards.details: The difference is not success but attempt. Most people, the chapter says, have not left Brixton; they have not even asked Cook's the price of a conducted tour. They excuse themselves by saying there are only twenty-four hours in the day, which hides that they have not started at all.

cards.title: The Wish Beyond the Formal Programme
cards.body: The unease springs from a fixed idea that you ought to do something in addition to your obligatory duties. Until you make an effort to satisfy that wish, you keep waiting for something that has not started.
cards.details: Maintaining health and comfort, paying debts, saving and increasing efficiency are difficult enough, yet success leaves the skeleton present. The wish outside the programme is common to those who have risen past a certain level; it is a form of the desire for knowledge, often taking literary shape, though literature is not the only well.

cards.body: Why does succeeding at one's ordinary duties fail to remove the uneasiness the chapter describes?
cards.answer: Because the uneasiness comes from a wish to do something in addition to the formal programme, not merely from duties left undone. Even when duties are met, the sense of waiting remains until an effort is made to satisfy that wish.

cards.body: The unease you feel is not a shortage of hours but an unsatisfied wish to do something beyond your duties. Success at duties will not silence it. The difference that matters is attempting, not arriving — so begin, instead of blaming the length of the day.

flashcards.q: What does the skeleton at the feast represent, and when does it appear?
flashcards.a: It represents the constant uneasiness that the years are slipping by while life remains out of working order. It interrupts laughter between theatre acts and questions what you have done with your youth and age while you wait for the last train.

flashcards.q: Why is the man who desires Mecca and never leaves Brixton more tormented than the man who sets out and fails to arrive?
flashcards.a: Because the difference between them is attempt, not success. The one who never leaves has not even asked the price of the journey, and covers his inaction with the excuse of only twenty-four hours in the day.

flashcards.q: Why does succeeding at duties such as health, paying debts and saving not remove the unease?
flashcards.a: Because the unease springs from a fixed idea that something ought to be done in addition to the obligatory programme. Until an effort is made toward that wish, one is simply waiting for something that has not started.

flashcards.q: If someone is efficient, solvent and comfortable yet still restless, what does this chapter suggest they should do?
flashcards.a: Make an effort toward the wish that lies outside their programme instead of waiting for it. The wish is a form of the desire for knowledge, often literary, though literature is not the only well.

chapters.title: Precautions Before Beginning
chapters.tldr: Before reorganising your day, accept that the task is punishingly hard, start at once instead of waiting for a better moment, and begin with small aims so that ardour does not burn out.
chapters.summary:
The chapter insists that the difficulty be accepted before anything else begins. No method will fit everything a person wants into one day; the honest beginner should expect sacrifice, steady effort and small returns rather than a painless system, and anyone unwilling to face discouragement is told not to start at all.

Beginning itself needs no technique: one simply begins, as one jumps into cold water, and nothing is gained by waiting for next week, since time cannot be squandered before it is used — every hour arrives fresh and unspoilt.

The last danger is ardour, which demands more and more and then dies. Start small, allow for accidents and human weakness, prefer a petty success to a glorious failure, because failure destroys confidence. Then the day's budget opens: seven hours of work, seven of sleep, eight unaccounted for.

cards.title: Accept the difficulty before starting
cards.body: There is no secret system for fitting everything you want into a day. The necessary first step is a calm acceptance that the task is extremely hard, demanding sacrifices and endless effort, and that no timetable written on paper will achieve the ideal.
cards.details: Anyone hoping for an easy, unfatiguing method is told to give up at once: the path is hard and stony, and you never quite arrive. If you cannot accept discouragement, disillusion and a small result for a big effort, you should not begin at all. Yet this bracing of the will is presented as the very thing that separates a person from a cat dozing by the fire.

cards.title: Just jump; today is unspoilt
cards.body: There is no magic method of beginning: you simply begin, as a man at the edge of a cold bath simply jumps. And there is no reason to wait for next week or tomorrow, because time cannot be wasted in advance — every hour arrives unspoilt.
cards.details: The supply of time is constant and cannot be squandered ahead of use: the next year, day and hour lie ready as perfect as if you had never misspent a moment. So you can turn over a new leaf every hour if you choose. Waiting is self-deception — if you fancy the water will be warmer next week, it will not; it will be colder.

cards.title: Beware ardour; aim for petty success
cards.body: Guard against your own ardour: it demands more and more, then dies suddenly once it tires. Undertake little at the start, allow for accidents and for human nature, and prefer a petty success to a glorious failure.
cards.details: A failure matters less in itself than for the loss of self-esteem and confidence it causes, and nothing fails like failure; most people are ruined by attempting too much. A glorious failure leads to nothing, while a petty success may lead to a success that is not petty. With that warning, the day's budget is opened: about seven hours earning a livelihood, seven in sleep, and eight still unaccounted for.

cards.body: Why does the book warn against starting with ambitious plans, even though ardour seems like a good thing?
cards.answer: Because ardour demands more and more, tires itself out, and then dies abruptly, leaving you with a failure that costs self-esteem and self-confidence. Nothing fails like failure, so an early collapse can end the whole attempt; starting small makes a first success likely.

cards.body: Expect the task to be hard and unglamorous, start today rather than waiting for a better moment, and begin with small aims: ardour inflates plans and then collapses, while a petty success builds the confidence a glorious failure destroys.

flashcards.q: Someone wants a painless method that squeezes everything they want into a single day. What does the chapter tell them?
flashcards.a: That no such method exists: the first step is accepting the task as extremely hard, full of sacrifice and endless effort with no real arrival, and someone who cannot accept discouragement and a small result for a big effort should not begin.

flashcards.q: Why does the chapter see no point in waiting until next week to start?
flashcards.a: Because time cannot be wasted in advance — every hour arrives unspoilt, as perfect as if you had never misspent a moment, so you can turn over a new leaf at any hour; the water will be colder next week, not warmer.

flashcards.q: Why is a petty success worth more than a glorious failure?
flashcards.a: A failure matters mainly for the loss of self-esteem and confidence it leaves behind, and nothing fails like failure; most people are ruined by attempting too much, while a petty success may grow into one that is not petty.

flashcards.q: How does the chapter finally divide up a day?
flashcards.a: Into roughly seven hours spent earning a livelihood, seven hours of sleep, and eight hours still unaccounted for.

chapters.title: The Cause Of The Troubles
chapters.tldr: The trouble begins when a man treats his ten-to-six job as the whole day and lets the sixteen hours that are truly his own slip away unused.
chapters.summary:
The argument has to begin somewhere concrete, so it begins with one man: a London clerk on ten to six, travelling fifty minutes each way. Money is set aside entirely, because for this purpose the man on a pound a week stands level with the millionaire. Every case is special, and only a real life, not a statistical average, can be reasoned about.

The mistake that man makes is to put the job at the centre. He calls ten to six 'the day' and counts the hours on either side as prologue and epilogue, even though he begins work reluctantly, ends it gladly, and never runs at full power while at it. Two-thirds of his existence are thus made to serve one-third he merely wants to get through. The remedy is to see the stretch from six in the evening to ten in the morning as a day within a day, sixteen hours belonging to body, soul and other people. Nor is the employer the loser, since the mind is refreshed by change rather than rest. Yet even these hours drain away unseen: on the platform, in a mental coma, five minutes are lost twice daily, and a man would cry out if a sovereign were changed on such terms.

cards.title: One case, not an average man
cards.body: There is no such thing as the average case, just as there is no average man, so the argument must follow a single individual: a London office worker on ten to six who spends fifty minutes travelling each way.
cards.details: That case is chosen because it comes as near the average as facts permit: some men must work longer for a living, others less. Money is deliberately set aside, since for this purpose the clerk earning a pound a week is exactly as well off as the millionaire in Carlton House-terrace. Every man's case is special, so the reasoning has to start from one concrete life rather than a statistical fiction.

cards.title: Making sixteen hours a prologue
cards.body: The typical man treats ten to six as "the day" and the ten hours before and six hours after as mere prologue and epilogue, so the hours that are truly his own are counted as margin.
cards.details: He begins his business functions reluctantly and as late as he can, ends them with joy and as early as he can, and his engines are seldom at full h.p. while he is at them — yet he gives that patch central prominence. Two-thirds of his existence are made subservient to one-third he only wants to get through. The correction is a day within a day, 6 p.m. to 10 a.m., sixteen hours for body, soul and fellow men, in which he is not a wage-earner. Nor does this drain the business eight: mental faculties do not tire like an arm or a leg; all they want is change, not rest, except in sleep.

cards.title: Robbed of five minutes twice a day
cards.body: He wastes little time before leaving the house at 9.10, but the moment the front door bangs his tireless mind goes idle: he walks to the station in a mental coma and waits on the platform while the railway company takes his time.
cards.details: On hundreds of suburban stations every morning men calmly stroll up and down while the companies unblushingly rob them, and hundreds of thousands of hours are lost daily because the man thinks so little of time that it never occurs to him to take easy precautions against losing it. He has a sovereign of time to spend each day and, in getting change for it, is content to lose heavily: five minutes twice a day is the equivalent of being charged three halfpence to change a sovereign, at which he would exclaim.

cards.body: The typical man objects that giving full energy to his sixteen free hours would lessen the value of his business eight. Why is he wrong, and what does that imply about how the mind should be used?
cards.answer: Because mental faculties do not tire like an arm or a leg: they are capable of continuous hard activity and want change rather than rest, except in sleep. So effort spent outside office hours does not subtract from the business day — it assuredly increases its value.

cards.body: Do not let a job you only want to get through sit at the centre of your life. The sixteen hours from six in the evening to ten in the morning are your own real day. And watch the small daily losses, like five idle minutes twice at the station, which are time spent at a shocking rate of exchange.

flashcards.q: Why does the chapter refuse to argue from an 'average man' and choose a London clerk instead?
flashcards.a: Because there is no average man and every case is special, so the reasoning must follow one concrete life. The clerk on ten to six with fifty minutes' travel is chosen only because he comes as near the average as facts allow.

flashcards.q: A man says his job is the real day and the hours around it are margin. What is wrong with that, and what should replace it?
flashcards.a: He is making two-thirds of his existence serve a third he only wants to get through, and giving it full power at neither end. He should treat 6 p.m. to 10 a.m. as a day within a day, sixteen hours that are truly his own.

flashcards.q: What does the loss of five minutes twice a day at the station illustrate?
flashcards.a: That a man values his time so little he takes no easy precaution against losing it. Losing five minutes twice daily is like paying three halfpence to change a sovereign, a rate he would protest at immediately.

chapters.title: Tennis And The Immortal Soul
chapters.tldr: The tiredness that supposedly rules out evening effort is a habit, so protect your best time — the morning train and a sacred ninety minutes every other evening — for consecutive cultivation of the mind.
chapters.summary:
The chapter starts by clearing away two excuses: the wrong use of time and the wrong belief about tiredness. The morning train, thirty or forty minutes of rare solitude, is too often handed over to newspapers, which are built for rapid reading in odd moments; reclaiming that time returns roughly three-quarters of an hour.

The second excuse is fatigue. It is not a fixed fact: when a theatre visit or a weekly chorus gives the evening a definite shape, the tiredness is forgotten and the evening feels long and energised. So at six o'clock you should admit you are not tired, arrange the evening so no meal cuts it in two, and secure three clear hours. From these, ninety minutes every other evening go to consecutive mental cultivation, while the other evenings stay free for friends, tennis, reading and pleasure. Those ninety minutes must be guarded as strictly as a rehearsal or a match.

cards.title: Newspapers Waste the Morning Train
cards.body: Do not spend the morning train on newspapers. Newspapers are made to be read rapidly; they belong in odd moments, not in thirty or forty consecutive minutes of rare solitude. Reclaim about three-quarters of an hour for use.
cards.details: The train compartment full of silent, withdrawn, smoking men is a place to immerse oneself in oneself; the reader who idly lingers over advertisements imagines a planet with 124 hours a day. The objection is not to newspapers but to giving them a secure block of time that could be put by for something else.

cards.title: Definite Engagements Erase Fatigue
cards.body: The tired feeling after office is not a fixed fact. When a theatre visit or operatic chorus gives a definite evening engagement, fatigue is forgotten and the evening seems long.
cards.details: For a theatre trip you rush to the suburbs, dress, rush back, stay on the stretch four or five hours, and take her home without spending forty minutes thinking about bed. Singing in a chorus twice a week for three months similarly slaves two hours and gives the whole day a glow and more intense vitality. Something definite at eventide can employ all your energy.

cards.title: The Sacred Ninety-Minute Evening
cards.body: At six o'clock, admit you are not tired and arrange the evening so no meal cuts it in two. This gives three clear hours; begin by using ninety minutes every other evening for consecutive mental cultivation.
cards.details: The remaining evenings stay free for friends, bridge, tennis, reading, gardening and pottering, and the weekend still offers forty-five hours from Saturday afternoon to Monday morning. Perseverance may make four or five evenings feel desirable. The ninety minutes must be treated as sacred as a dramatic rehearsal or a tennis match, and you must learn to say "I have to work."
steps: At six o'clock, face facts and admit you are not tired, because the fatigue is a habit rather than a real limit.
Arrange the evening so a meal does not split it, protecting a clear expanse of time.
Secure at least three clear hours instead of letting the evening dissolve.
For a start, reserve ninety minutes every other evening for important, consecutive cultivation of the mind.
Keep the remaining evenings for friends, bridge, tennis, domestic scenes, reading and other pleasures.
Treat those ninety minutes as sacred as a dramatic rehearsal or a tennis match.
Say "I have to work" rather than using tennis as the excuse.

cards.body: Why is the six o'clock tired feeling unreliable, and what should you do with the evening once you stop trusting it?
cards.answer: It disappears when a definite engagement such as theatre or chorus demands energy, so it is a habit rather than a true limit. Admit you are not tired, arrange an unbroken evening, and reserve ninety minutes every other evening for sustained mental work while keeping other evenings free.

cards.body: Fatigue after work is a habit, not a limit. Claim the morning train instead of the newspapers, and reserve ninety minutes every other evening for continuous mental work — defended as firmly as a tennis match, with the honest answer "I have to work".

flashcards.q: Why does the chapter object to reading newspapers on the morning train?
flashcards.a: Newspapers are made to be read rapidly and belong in odd moments. Spending thirty or forty consecutive minutes of rare solitude on them, and even lingering over advertisements, throws away about three-quarters of an hour that could be used for something else.

flashcards.q: What does the theatre trip and the weekly chorus show about feeling tired after the office?
flashcards.a: That the fatigue is not a fixed fact: a definite evening engagement makes it disappear, the evening feels long, and the whole day gains a glow and more intense vitality.

flashcards.q: How should the ninety minutes of mental cultivation be set up and defended?
flashcards.a: At six o'clock admit you are not tired and arrange the evening so no meal splits it, giving three clear hours; then take ninety minutes every other evening and treat them as sacred as a dramatic rehearsal or a tennis match.

flashcards.q: A friend invites you to play tennis on one of your cultivation evenings. What does the chapter tell you to answer?
flashcards.a: Say "I have to work" instead of using tennis as the excuse, because the ninety minutes must be as fixed an engagement as a rehearsal or a match.

chapters.title: Remember Human Nature
chapters.tldr: Aim at only seven and a half hours a week over six days, treat any extra as a windfall, and start humbly enough that the change of habits cannot fail.
chapters.summary: The programme belongs to six days, not seven: a regular day of idleness has real moral worth, and any time added beyond that should be counted as a windfall, so that returning to six days never feels like a loss. What is aimed at is small — half an hour on six mornings and ninety minutes on three evenings, seven and a half hours a week. Against a hundred and sixty-eight hours that looks negligible, yet, like brief daily exercise, it enlivens the whole week, and more time would only give more. Clearing even this much is hard, because the hours are already occupied and habits resist change, and a failed plan wounds the self-respect that purposefulness rests on. So begin humbly and quietly, judge yourself only after three months, and in the evening protect a window far longer than the task.

cards.title: Confine the programme to six days
cards.body: The formal super-programme should normally occupy six days a week, not seven. If you want to extend it, extend it only in proportion to your actual wish, and treat the extra time as a windfall rather than regular income.
cards.details: The reason is that a recurring day of idleness has real moral value, appreciated most by those who have lived at full stretch seven days a week for years. Only abounding youth with exceptional energy and desire for effort should keep going day in, day out. Counting extra time as a windfall matters because it lets you return to six days without feeling poorer or like a backslider.

cards.title: Seven and a half hours can renew the week
cards.body: Half an hour on six mornings plus one and a half hours on three evenings totals seven and a half hours a week — and that is enough to be aimed at for now.
cards.details: The objection is obvious: seven and a half hours out of a hundred and sixty-eight looks like nothing. The claim is that using them fully quickens the whole life of the week, adds zest, and increases interest even in the most banal occupations. The analogy is physical exercise: ten minutes morning and evening visibly affects health and strength every hour of the day, so an average of over an hour a day given to the mind should similarly enliven the whole activity of the mind. More time would give greater results, but the beginning is deliberately small.

cards.title: Clearing time costs sacrifice and volition
cards.body: Even seven and a half hours is passably hard to clear from the jungle, because the time was already spent doing something, and doing something else means changing habits.
cards.details: You may have spent your time badly, but you did spend it, and to do something else requires a change of habits — which are the very dickens to change. Any change, even for the better, brings drawbacks and discomforts; you cannot devote the hours to serious continuous effort and still live your old life. Because failure in such an enterprise has an almost disastrous effect, the advice is a very humble, quiet, unostentatious start: self-respect is at the root of all purposefulness, and a planned failure wounds it desperately. Only after three conscientious months may you tell yourself what wondrous things you are capable of.

cards.title: Budgeting the evening in advance
cards.body: Allow much more clock time than the work itself requires, so accidents and human nature cannot destroy the plan.
cards.details: The final suggestion concerns the evenings: the ninety minutes of task should be given a window far larger than ninety minutes. Allowing from 9 to 11.30 for a task of ninety minutes builds in the chance of accidents and the resistance of human nature, so the session survives a late start or an interruption.
steps: Decide the length of the actual task you intend to do, here ninety minutes.
Choose an evening window much longer than that task, here from 9 to 11.30.
Protect the whole window rather than the task alone, so accidents and human nature do not break the programme.

cards.body: Why does the author insist on starting with a small, unostentatious programme rather than with all the time you could theoretically spare?
cards.answer: Because failure in a deliberately planned enterprise wounds self-respect, and self-respect is the root of all purposefulness. A humble beginning that you actually keep protects it; after three months of conscientiously giving seven and a half hours a week you can raise your ambitions.

cards.body: Aim small: seven and a half hours a week, spread over six days, with the seventh free. Treat any extra time as a windfall. Expect clearing those hours to cost you old habits, so start so quietly that failure is unlikely, and give each evening session a window much longer than the work itself.

flashcards.q: Why keep the programme to six days a week instead of seven?
flashcards.a: Because a recurring day of idleness has a real moral value, and treating any extra time as a windfall rather than regular income means you can drop back to six days without feeling like a backslider.

flashcards.q: Seven and a half hours is nothing against a hundred and sixty-eight — why is it still worth aiming at?
flashcards.a: Like ten minutes of exercise morning and evening that affects every hour of the day, an average of just over an hour a day on the mind quickens the whole week and adds zest even to banal occupations. More time would give more, but the start is deliberately small.

flashcards.q: You plan ninety minutes of serious work on Tuesday evening. How should you schedule it?
flashcards.a: Give the ninety-minute task a far larger window, such as 9 to 11.30, so a late start or an interruption cannot destroy the session; protect the window, not just the task.

flashcards.q: Why start quietly and modestly rather than with an ambitious plan?
flashcards.a: Because failure here is almost disastrous and self-respect is at the root of all purposefulness, so a planned failure wounds it desperately. Prove yourself over three conscientious months before expecting wonders.

chapters.title: Controlling The Mind
chapters.tldr: The mind can and must be trained like a muscle: choose a subject when you leave the house, haul your attention back every time it strays, and concentrate on something worth thinking about, since this discipline is the first requirement of a full life.
chapters.summary:
Everything a person feels, enjoys or suffers happens inside the brain, so the power to give that brain a task and make it obey is the most valuable skill there is. It is not a fixed gift handed out at birth: people who say they cannot concentrate are wrong, because the thinking machine can be controlled if you decide to control it, and without that control real living is impossible. The mind therefore deserves the daily fuss we already give the far coarser machinery of the body — and it needs no equipment at all.

The training itself happens on the way to work. Pick a subject as you leave the house and keep it there; the mind will bolt within yards, and the work is to drag it back each time, perhaps forty times before the station. No book or apparatus is required, so it can be done in the street or on the train without anyone noticing. Since the discipline is what counts, the subject should be worth the effort: a short chapter of Marcus Aurelius or Epictetus read in the evening, held in the mind the next morning — plain sense for ordinary people, and a cure for worry.

cards.title: Mind control is possible and essential
cards.body: Everything we feel, enjoy or suffer happens inside the brain, so the ability to dictate what the brain does is the most valuable skill a person can have — and it can be acquired, not just inherited.
cards.details: People complain they lack the power to concentrate, assuming it is a fixed gift; the text calls it perfectly possible to control the thinking machine if you choose to. Without the power to give the brain a task and ensure obedience, true life is impossible: mind control is the first element of a full existence. So the first business of the day should be putting the mind through its paces, just as people already fuss over the far less delicate machinery of the body — except that the mind needs no outside help at all.

cards.title: The daily concentration exercise
cards.body: Train concentration on the way to work: pick a subject when you leave the house, and every time the mind escapes, drag it back — forty times if necessary — until it obeys.
cards.details: The exercise requires no tools, not even a book, and can be done in the street, on the platform, in the train or strap-hanging on the Underground: unlike carrying dumb-bells or an encyclopaedia, nobody can see you and nobody can laugh. It is not easy. You will not have gone ten yards before the mind skips away; bring it back by the scruff of the neck, and expect about forty recaptures before you reach the station. Perseverance is the only secret, and the text insists you cannot fail if you keep it up.
steps: On leaving the house, choose a subject — any subject to begin with — and concentrate the mind on it.
The moment the mind skips away to something else, bring it back at once, so the exercise stays continuous.
Expect roughly forty such recaptures before you reach the station, and do not despair at the number.
Repeat the practice every day, since perseverance is the only secret and success is guaranteed to those who continue.
Do it wherever you happen to be — street, platform, train — because no tools and no book are needed.

cards.title: Concentrate on something worth thinking
cards.body: Since the disciplining of the thinking machine is what counts, whichever subject you use, choose a useful one: read a short chapter of Marcus Aurelius or Epictetus in the evening and concentrate on it the next morning.
cards.details: The objection that this is not "in your line" is dismissed: the suggestion is not the author's own but that of sensible, practical, hard-headed men, offered second-hand. The recommended chapters are short and, the text claims, bursting with plain common sense applicable to the daily life of ordinary people who hate airs and pose. The reward is not only a trained mind: the process is said to cure half the evils of life, especially worry, called a miserable, avoidable, shameful disease.

cards.body: Your mind keeps slipping away ten yards from home during the exercise. According to the text, what should you do, and why is failure not really a risk?
cards.answer: Bring it back immediately and keep going, expecting about forty recaptures before reaching the station; the exercise only fails if you stop. The disquieting-letter case proves the mind can hold one subject without interruption when it is made to.

cards.body: Concentration is a trainable skill, not a birthright, and nothing else in life works without it. Practise daily on the way to work: hold one chosen subject and bring the mind back every time it wanders, forty times if need be. Make the subject worth thinking about.

flashcards.q: Why is the power to control the mind called the first element of a full existence?
flashcards.a: Because everything we feel, enjoy or suffer takes place inside the brain, so being able to give the brain a task and ensure its obedience is what makes true life possible. It is treated as an acquirable skill, not a fixed gift, even though people complain they simply lack it.

flashcards.q: Describe exactly what you do during the concentration exercise on the way to work.
flashcards.a: On leaving the house you choose a subject and concentrate on it; the moment the mind skips away you bring it back at once, expecting roughly forty recaptures before reaching the station. You repeat this every day, wherever you are, and perseverance is the only secret.

flashcards.q: Why can this exercise be done in the street or on a crowded train when other training cannot?
flashcards.a: It needs no tools and no book — not even an encyclopaedia or dumb-bells — so nobody can see what you are doing and nobody can laugh at you. The whole apparatus is your own attention.

flashcards.q: Why does it matter which subject you concentrate on, and what is recommended?
flashcards.a: The disciplining of the thinking machine is what counts whichever subject you use, so a useful one costs nothing extra: read a short chapter of Marcus Aurelius or Epictetus in the evening and concentrate on it the next morning. Such chapters are short and full of plain common sense for ordinary people, and the practice is said to cure half the evils of life, especially worry.

chapters.title: The Reflective Mood
chapters.tldr: Concentration is only the preliminary skill; the real daily work is the reflective mood — candid self-examination of your happiness, direction, reason, principles and conduct, for which no book is a substitute.
chapters.summary:
Concentration is merely the preliminary, like practising scales on a piano; once the mind obeys, it must be applied to a prolonged study whose subject is oneself. Sensible people of every age agree that this course is not literature, art, history or science but "Man, know thyself" — universally praised, rarely practised. What the well-intentioned person most lacks is the reflective mood: thought about his own happiness, the direction he is taking, the share reason has in his actions, and whether his conduct matches his principles.

Happiness, moreover, does not come from pleasure but from reason developed and conduct adjusted to principles, and that adjustment happens only through daily examination and resolution. The specific principles matter less than the agreement between them and one's deeds: martyrs are happy because the two coincide, while burglars are sorrowful because their principles contradict their trade. Books by Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, Pascal, La Bruyère and Emerson can shape principles, but nothing replaces an honest daily look at oneself — best taken in the solitude of the evening journey home.

cards.title: Self-knowledge is the real course of study
cards.body: Concentration is only a preliminary, like scales on the piano. Once the mind has learned to obey, it must be put to work on a prolonged course of study whose subject is oneself.
cards.details: All sensible people of all ages agree on what that course is, and it is not literature, art, history or any science: it is "Man, know thyself" — a phrase everyone acknowledges as valuable and only the most sagacious actually practise. What the average well-intentioned person most lacks is the reflective mood: reflection on his own happiness, on the main direction he is going, on the share reason has in determining his actions, and on the relation between his principles and his conduct.

cards.title: Happiness comes from conduct matching principles
cards.body: Happiness does not spring from procuring physical or mental pleasure but from the development of reason and the adjustment of conduct to principles — and conduct only adjusts through daily examination, reflection and resolution.
cards.details: The particular principles are not the point: they might even justify burglary. What makes burglars permanently sorrowful is that their principles contradict burglary, whereas a genuine believer in its moral excellence would find penal servitude simply happy years — all martyrs are happy because conduct and principles agree. So whoever admits that happiness depends on this, yet gives no part of the day to considering reason, principles and conduct, admits he regularly leaves undone the one act necessary to the thing he is striving for.

cards.title: Consulting reason about an over-cooked steak
cards.body: When you get cross with the waiter over an over-cooked steak, summoning reason to the cabinet-room of your mind shows that the waiter did not cook the steak and that your anger changes nothing.
cards.details: Reason plays a far smaller part in our lives than we fancy: we are much more instinctive than reasonable, and the less we reflect the less reasonable we become. Consulted, she will point out that the waiter had no control over the cooking, and that even if he alone were to blame, anger gained nothing — you lost your dignity, looked a fool before sensible men and soured the waiter while the steak stayed the same. The result, at no charge: stay calm and kindly, treat him as a fellow-creature, and politely insist on a fresh steak.

cards.title: Books help, but self-examination is indispensable
cards.body: Books such as Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, Pascal, La Bruyère and Emerson help form and modify principles, but no reading replaces a daily, candid, honest examination of what one has recently done and is about to do.
cards.details: The author will not travel without his Marcus Aurelius, and still insists that books cannot substitute for the steady looking at oneself in the face, disconcerting though the sight may be. For the time of this business he proposes the solitude of the evening journey home, since a reflective mood naturally follows the exertion of having earned the day's living; the paper can be read while waiting for dinner. But attend to it at some hour of the day you must.

cards.body: Why can no amount of reading Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius or Emerson do the work of the daily examination of yourself?
cards.answer: Because books only supply principles; they do not compare your principles with your actual conduct. Only the daily, candid examination of what you have just done and are about to do makes conduct accord with principles, and conduct that does not accord with them makes a silly, unhappy life.

cards.body: Train concentration only as a means; then spend part of every day examining yourself — your happiness, your direction, how much reason rules you, and whether your conduct matches your principles. Happiness depends on that fit, and no book can do the examining for you.

flashcards.q: Why is concentration described as only a preliminary, like scales on the piano?
flashcards.a: Because it is just the training that teaches the mind to obey; once that is achieved, the mind must be put to work on the real course of study, whose subject is oneself.

flashcards.q: According to the chapter, what actually produces happiness, and why does that make daily reflection necessary?
flashcards.a: Happiness comes from reason developed and conduct adjusted to principles, not from physical or mental pleasure. Since conduct only adjusts through daily examination, reflection and resolution, skipping it means leaving undone the one act the goal depends on.

flashcards.q: What does reason show you when you are angry about an over-cooked steak, and what should you do instead?
flashcards.a: That the waiter did not cook the steak and that anger changes nothing — it only costs you dignity and sours him while the steak stays the same. Stay calm and kindly, treat him as a fellow-creature, and politely insist on a fresh steak.

flashcards.q: What role do books such as Marcus Aurelius or Epictetus play, and what can they not replace?
flashcards.a: They help form and modify one's principles, but no reading can substitute for a daily, candid and honest examination of what one has recently done and is about to do.

chapters.title: Interest In The Arts
chapters.tldr: Evening self-improvement fails on a false choice between doing nothing and studying literature; any art you already enjoy can be learned systematically, with a primer, chosen concerts, and a year of short evenings.
chapters.summary:
The chapter attacks the assumption that a worthwhile evening means either literature or nothing. Because people equate reading with belles-lettres, they conclude they have no taste for study, when in fact a book on bridge, boat-sailing or music is a book too, and needs no appetite for poetry to be enjoyed.

Music shows how much there is to gain. A concertgoer may be genuinely moved yet hear only an agreeable blur, unable to name the instruments playing the opening theme of the C minor symphony. A cheap primer with photographs of instruments and seating plans turns that blur into separate voices with separate functions.

The method generalises. Take the art you already like, admit you understand it only vaguely, and read a primer meant for listeners or viewers rather than performers. Attend what you already attend, but hunt for detail; then select future concerts yourself from what you have learned, and specialise in one form or composer. Forty-eight weeks of three brief evenings buys real knowledge — never performance.

cards.title: Literature is not the only study
cards.body: People drift into evening idleness because they see only two options: doing nothing or studying literature. That is a false choice. Books about non-literary subjects — bridge, boat-sailing, music — are still books, and you read them without needing any love of literature.
cards.details: The rule is a distinction: separate literature itself from books that treat of subjects not literary. Nobody refuses to read the best book on bridge because they dislike poetry. The practical consequence is that "I don't care for reading" usually means "I don't care for belles-lettres", which blocks nothing; and not loving literature is neither a crime nor a sign of imbecility, whatever the mandarins of literature may pronounce about Wordsworth and Tennyson.

cards.title: From a confused mass to an orchestra
cards.body: You already have a genuine taste for music — the conductor's programmes prove it — even though you cannot play a note. What you lack is trained attention: you hear an agreeable blur instead of separate instruments with separate functions.
cards.details: The test case is the opening theme of the C minor symphony: you cannot name the instruments playing it, though the work has thrilled you and you have praised it as a "jolly fine thing". Read Krehbiel's "How to Listen to Music" — cheaper than a stall at the Alhambra, with photographs of the instruments and plans of orchestral seating — and the next promenade concert changes. You spy out the instruments, listen for each sound, see why an oboe player earns more than a fiddler, and live there instead of existing in a beatific coma.

cards.title: Lay systematic foundations in an art
cards.body: A year of short, regular evenings, directed by a good primer and by concerts you choose yourself, is enough to genuinely know something about an art — even if you never learn to perform.
cards.details: The arithmetic in the text is forty-eight weeks of three brief evenings each, combined with studying programmes and attending concerts picked out of your growing knowledge. Note what it does not require: pianistic skill, or the ability to play "The Maiden's Prayer". The same method transfers to other arts, begun with books like Clermont Witt's "How to Look at Pictures" or Russell Sturgis's "How to Judge Architecture" — beginnings only, but vitalising ones, with London supplying the material.
steps: Pick the art you already enjoy and admit you understand only vaguely.
Read a primer built for listeners or viewers, not for performers, such as Krehbiel on listening.
Attend the concerts or exhibitions you already go to, but now hunting for details.
Identify individual instruments or elements and the function each group performs.
Choose your next concerts or shows yourself, out of what you have learned.
Specialise: follow one form, such as the symphony, or one composer.
Give it forty-eight weeks of three brief evenings, and expect knowledge, not performance.

cards.body: A reader says: "I go to concerts and I love the music, so I already get everything out of them. What would reading a book about the orchestra actually change?"
cards.answer: It changes listening from passive enjoyment to active perception. Where the orchestra was a heterogeneous mass of pleasant sound, it becomes a balanced organism whose groups each have an indispensable function; you spy out the instruments, listen for their separate sounds, and can tell a French horn from an English horn. The concerts become experiences you live at instead of merely exist at, and that trained attention is the foundation of systematic knowledge of music.

cards.body: You need no talent and no love of literature to learn an art. Take the one you already enjoy, admit you only half understand it, read a primer written for audiences rather than performers, then attend with your attention sharpened and choose what to see next. Three short evenings a week for forty-eight weeks is enough to know something real.

flashcards.a: It usually means a dislike of belles-lettres only, and books on bridge, boat-sailing or music are still books that require no love of literature.

chapters.title: Nothing In Life Is Humdrum
chapters.tldr: Nothing in life is humdrum once you habitually perceive cause and effect — in human nature, in the changing world, and in your own trade.
chapters.summary:
The chapter's central claim is that the most valuable perception a person can cultivate is the continual sense that nothing happens without a cause. Whoever habitually asks why things happen becomes both large-minded and large-hearted: he stops being shocked and pained by human behaviour as though he were a stranger in a strange land, and can even absorb a stolen watch by reflecting that the thief was made by heredity and environment, which makes bitterness impossible.

The same habit makes the world picturesque rather than monotonous. To someone imbued with development, the sea is not a fixed view costing three shillings third-class in August, but an element that was vapour, then boiling water, and will inevitably be ice — a liquid merely on its way to being solid. That durable satisfaction is what all science is for, and it works on ordinary city life too: a traffic block in Oxford Street pushes travellers under cellars and drains and raises rents in Shepherd's Bush. Study your own trade's causes for ninety minutes every other evening and it gains zest; art or literature is not required to live fully.

cards.title: Nothing Happens Without a Cause
cards.body: The most important of all perceptions is the continual perception of cause and effect: nothing happens without a cause. Getting this into your head makes you not only large-minded but large-hearted.
cards.details: It cures the absurd air of being always shocked and pained by the curiousness of life, the way people live amid human nature as if it were a foreign country full of awful customs; at maturity one should be ashamed of being a stranger in a strange land. A stolen watch hurts, but one reflects that the thief became a thief from heredity and environment, as interesting as they are scientifically comprehensible, and buys another with a philosophy that makes bitterness impossible.

cards.title: The Sea as Vapour, Water, Ice
cards.body: To a man imbued with development, the sea is not a monotonous spectacle but an element that was vapour the day before yesterday, boiling yesterday, and will inevitably be ice tomorrow.
cards.details: The man to whom evolution is only a name sees a grandiose, monotonous view that costs three shillings third-class return in August. The other perceives that a liquid is merely something on its way to be solid, and is penetrated by a sense of the tremendous, changeful picturesqueness of life. Cultivating this appreciation is called the end of all science, and nothing affords a more durable satisfaction.

cards.title: Study Your Own Trade's Causes
cards.body: Nothing is humdrum once you trace causes: a traffic block in Oxford Street pushed travellers under cellars and drains, and rents rose in Shepherd's Bush. Apply the same study to your own trade and it gains zest.
cards.details: Clerks lunching at a Lyons put two and two together: the Two-penny Tube caused the demand for wigwams in Shepherd's Bush, and that demand caused the rise in the price of wigwams. The method is to study your field for ninety minutes every other evening — the estate agent the London property question, the bank clerk Bagehot's Lombard Street — or, penned in town, to net the moths beating about a gas lamp and co-ordinate what you learn. Devotion to art or literature is not required to live fully.

cards.body: Your work feels humdrum and you care nothing for art or literature. What does the chapter tell you to do, and why would it work?
cards.answer: Study the cause and effect running through your own field, ninety minutes every other evening, as the estate agent studies London property or the bank clerk reads Lombard Street. Once you see the chains of cause behind the daily scene, nothing looks humdrum and your business gains zest.

cards.body: Train yourself to see causes everywhere: in other people's conduct, in the changing state of things, and in your own daily work. Once you trace why things happen, nothing looks dull or shocking any more, and you can study your own trade for ninety minutes every other evening to keep that zest alive.

flashcards.a: Because it replaces shock at human behaviour with comprehension: even a thief can be seen as a product of heredity and environment, so the bitterness of feeling wronged becomes impossible.

flashcards.q: How does a sense of development change what someone sees in the sea?
flashcards.a: Instead of a grandiose, monotonous view, he sees an element that was vapour the day before yesterday, is liquid now, and will inevitably be ice — a liquid merely on its way to being solid.

flashcards.q: Why is a traffic block in Oxford Street worth studying rather than merely endured?
flashcards.a: Because tracing its causes and consequences shows nothing is humdrum: travellers were pushed under cellars and drains, and rents rose in Shepherd's Bush as a result.

flashcards.q: What practical routine does the chapter recommend for bringing zest to your own trade?
flashcards.a: Study your own field for ninety minutes every other evening — the estate agent the London property question, the bank clerk Bagehot's Lombard Street — tracing causes rather than just noting events.

chapters.title: Serious Reading
chapters.tldr: Serious reading means giving your daily ninety minutes to material that strains the mind — poetry first, then history or philosophy — narrowed to a fixed subject and paired with at least forty-five minutes of hard reflection.
chapters.summary:
Mental cultivation depends on strain, and that single criterion decides what belongs in the reading hour. A good novel carries you forward without effort, so it is excluded — not because novels are inferior, but because they cannot supply the resistance the mind needs to grow.

Poetry imposes the heaviest strain and returns the most, so it comes first. If poetry feels closed to you, Hazlitt's essay on the nature of poetry dissolves the fear, and Browning's Aurora Leigh, read simply for its story and social ideas, is the honest test of whether you really dislike it. Should poetry remain repellent, turn to history or philosophy instead — but only under two rules: confine yourself to a limited period, subject or single author for a set stretch of time, and think as well as read, giving what you read at least forty-five minutes of tiring reflection. Without that thinking, the time is mostly wasted.

cards.title: Good novels give no mental strain
cards.body: Novels are excluded from serious reading because a good novel demands no strain: it rushes you forward like a skiff down a stream, leaving you breathless but unexhausted. Mental cultivation depends on the feeling of strain, which a novel cannot supply.
cards.details: The exclusion is not a judgement on the genre: some of the great literature of the world is prose fiction, and you should read novels. But only the bad parts of Meredith are difficult, and the best novels involve the least strain — you do not set your teeth in order to read Anna Karenina. Since a task one part of you wants and another shirks is the key factor in cultivating the mind, novels belong outside the ninety minutes, not inside them.

cards.title: Breaking into poetry through Hazlitt
cards.body: Poetry produces the severest mental strain of any literature and yields the highest pleasure and wisdom, so read it before anything else. If it is a sealed book to you, enter it by a fixed route.
cards.details: Hazlitt's essay is the best thing of its kind in English: after reading it, poetry stops looking like a mediaeval torture, a mad elephant or a gun that goes off by itself and kills at forty paces, and you want some before your next meal. Aurora Leigh, a novel in verse by E. B. Browning, finer than anything by George Eliot, the Brontes or Austen, is the honest test — more than one person has found through it that in assuming they hated poetry they were entirely mistaken.
steps: Read Hazlitt's famous essay on the nature of poetry in general, to clear away the idea that poetry is a form of torture.
If the essay inspires you, make your commencement with purely narrative poetry.
Decide to read Aurora Leigh by E. B. Browning through, even if you die for it.
Forget that it is fine poetry and read it simply for the story and the social ideas.
When you have finished, ask yourself honestly whether you still dislike poetry.

cards.title: Limit your subject and reflect on it
cards.body: If poetry stays antagonistic to you, take up history or philosophy instead. Two rules then decide whether the reading does any good: define the direction and scope of your effort, and think as well as read.
cards.details: Scope means choosing a limited period, a limited subject or a single author — say to yourself "I will know something about the French Revolution, or the rise of railways, or the works of John Keats" — and confining yourself to that choice for a period settled beforehand, since there is much pleasure in being a specialist. Thinking means giving at least forty-five minutes of careful, fatiguing reflection, an awful bore at first, to what you read; without it your ninety minutes are chiefly wasted and you merely fly through literature for the sake of motion. The pace will be slow; that does not matter.

cards.body: Why does spending the ninety minutes on a great novel fail to cultivate the mind, while spending them on poetry succeeds?
cards.answer: Cultivation depends on the feeling of strain, of a task one part of you wants and another shirks. A good novel carries you along effortlessly, so that feeling never arises; poetry imposes the severest mental strain, which is why it belongs in the ninety minutes and novels do not.

cards.body: Choose reading that strains you. Novels, however good, don't count because they carry you along. Begin with poetry — Hazlitt to open the door, Aurora Leigh as the honest test. If poetry fails, take history or philosophy, narrow the field to one period, subject or author, and give at least forty-five minutes of hard thinking to it.

flashcards.q: Why are novels left out of serious reading, and is that a judgement on the genre?
flashcards.a: Because a good novel produces no mental strain — it carries you along like a skiff down a stream — and cultivation depends on feeling strain. It is not a judgement: great literature includes prose fiction and you should read novels, just outside the ninety minutes.

flashcards.q: How would you honestly test whether you actually dislike poetry?
flashcards.a: Read Hazlitt's essay on the nature of poetry to clear away the idea that poetry is a form of torture, then start with purely narrative poetry and read Aurora Leigh through for the story and social ideas. Afterwards ask yourself honestly whether you still dislike poetry.

flashcards.q: You have settled on history. What two rules decide whether the reading does any good, and what does each require?
flashcards.a: Define the direction and scope of your effort — a limited period, a limited subject or a single author, held to for a period settled beforehand. And think as well as read, giving at least forty-five minutes of careful, fatiguing reflection to what you read.

chapters.title: Dangers To Avoid
chapters.tldr: Using your hours well can make you a smug prig or a slave to your own timetable, and it is more likely to fail through trying to do too much at a rush than through laziness — so attempt less, start slowly, and hold your programme lightly.
chapters.summary:
Time-keeping brings two temptations of character before it brings any benefit. The first is self-importance: a person who has discovered a way to use hours well easily turns into a prig, humourless and aggrieved that others are not impressed. The corrective is scale — the material is your own time, not other people's, and the world got along before your budget existed. Say nothing about your system; looking after yourself exhausts your commission.

The second is rigidity. A programme deserves respect but not worship, and there is a fine line: treat it as a fetish and you become the wife who says a thing is "quite out of the question" because the dog must be walked at eight; neglect it entirely and it is a joke. The third and cruellest danger is rush, which narrows life to the next obligation. Rebellion does not mend it, since the fault is an overfull programme; only attempting less does. Where the programme cannot be cut, deliberately waste five minutes in mental quiet. And go slowly at the start, finishing each task so that confidence survives.

cards.title: The first danger is becoming a prig
cards.body: Using your time well can turn you into a prig: a pompous fool who gives himself airs of superior wisdom, has lost his sense of humour, and is gravely displeased that the whole world is not impressed by his discovery.
cards.details: The remedy is to remember that the material you deal with is your own time, not other people's. The earth rolled on comfortably before you began balancing a budget of hours and will keep rolling whether or not you succeed as its chancellor of the exchequer. So do not chatter about what you are doing, and do not wear a pained sadness at the sight of a world wasting its hours — taking care of yourself will turn out to be quite all you can do.

cards.title: Respect the programme, do not worship it
cards.body: A programme of daily employ must be respected but not treated as a fetish; it is not a religion, and one must live with neither too much nor too little elasticity.
cards.details: The book's example is the martyred wife: Arthur always takes the dog out at eight and always begins to read at a quarter to nine, so "it's quite out of the question that we should..." — the note of absolute finality in her voice reveals the ridiculous tragedy of a life enslaved to a chariot. Yet a programme untended ceases to be anything but a poor joke, and hitting exactly the right degree of deference is scarcely the simple affair it looks to the inexperienced.

cards.title: Rush, and failing at the start
cards.body: A policy of rush imprisons you in what you must do next; the cure is not occasional rebellion but attempting less. And at the start, go absurdly slowly and regularly.
cards.details: Breaking the programme now and then mends nothing, because the evil comes from originally filling the programme till it runs over; reconstitute it and attempt less. If you refuse to modify it, spend five minutes in perfect mental quiescence between one portion and the next — waste them with full consciousness of wasting them. A failure at the commencement can kill the newborn impulse, so make the first lap slow but regular, finish the task at all costs for the immense gain in self-confidence, and choose your first evening occupations by taste alone: street-cries over philosophy if that is what you like.

cards.body: Why does deliberately breaking your programme now and then fail to cure the feeling of being rushed?
cards.answer: Because the problem is not inflexible persistence but having attempted too much in the first place — the programme was filled until it ran over. The cure is to reconstitute the programme and attempt less, not to rebel against it occasionally.

cards.body: Guard against smugness: the schedule is yours alone, so don't preach it. Respect your programme without becoming its slave. If you are always rushing, the answer is not occasional revolt but attempting less; if your first efforts fail, you may lose the impulse altogether, so begin absurdly slowly, complete each task for the confidence it gives, and pick that first evening's activity purely by taste.

flashcards.q: What exactly is the danger of becoming a prig, and what is the remedy?
flashcards.a: You become a pompous fool who has lost his sense of humour and is displeased that the world is unimpressed by your discovery. The remedy is to remember the material is your own time, not other people's, so say nothing about it and accept that looking after yourself is all you can manage.

flashcards.q: Why does breaking the programme now and then fail to cure a life of rush?
flashcards.a: Because the evil comes from having filled the programme till it runs over, so occasional rebellion changes nothing. The programme has to be reconstituted with less in it; if you will not cut it, spend five minutes in perfect mental quiescence between portions, consciously wasting them.

flashcards.q: What does the example of the wife of Arthur's household illustrate?
flashcards.a: Her "it's quite out of the question that we should..." shows the ridiculous tragedy of a life enslaved to its own timetable. It is the excess of rigidity — treating the programme as a fetish rather than something to be respected — and the book notes that hitting the right degree of deference is far from simple.

flashcards.q: How should you plan the very first evening of a new habit, and why?
flashcards.a: Go absurdly slowly and regularly, and finish the task at all costs for the self-confidence it brings, because a failure at the commencement can kill the newborn impulse. Choose the occupation by taste alone — street-cries over philosophy, if that is what you like.

glossary.definition: The morning refill of twenty-four hours, distributed equally to everyone, with no extra hour for genius and no borrowing against tomorrow.
Ninety minutes every other evening given to connected mental work, guarded as strictly as a rehearsal or a match.
The planned use of hours over six days: half an hour on six mornings and ninety minutes on three evenings, with extra time counted as a windfall.
Thought about one's own happiness, direction, share of reason, and whether conduct matches principles.
The resistance the mind needs to grow; the criterion deciding what belongs in the reading hour.
Reading that strains the mind, with poetry first and at least forty-five minutes of hard reflection; effortless novels are excluded.
